summary: This standards-track document addresses the size and freshness of the learning table in edge RBridges by letting endnodes volunteer to do their own learning and TRILL encapsulation. Such an endnode is called a Smart Endnode. It is attached only to a single edge RBridge that can accept or reject this.

eli5.summary: Instead of the front desk remembering every guest, smart guests keep their own notes and wrap their own mail, which keeps the desk's list shorter.

questions: what is a trill smart endnode
how to reduce rbridge learning table size
what is a smart-hello in trill
how do smart endnodes avoid mac flip-flopping
what are smart-parameters and smart-mac tlvs
subtitle: Lets a host volunteer to do its own TRILL learning and encapsulation, easing the load on its edge switch.

tldr.problem: An edge RBridge must keep a table of remote MAC addresses and their egress switches, which can grow very large and can go stale when an address moves, so traffic gets lost.
tldr.mechanism: An endnode announces itself as a Smart Endnode with a Smart-Hello, then keeps its own table and encapsulates and decapsulates TRILL frames using the nickname of its attached edge RBridge.
tldr.outcome: The edge RBridge's table stays smaller and no extra nicknames are used. The trade-off is that Smart Endnodes can forge headers, so they must be trusted or authenticated.

today: RFC 8384 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Endnode Table Problem
sections.content:
TRILL gives optimal pair-wise forwarding using IS-IS link-state routing and a header with a hop count. An edge RBridge is one that attaches to endnodes. Traditionally it is the edge RBridge that encapsulates native Ethernet frames and decapsulates TRILL packets.

To encapsulate efficiently, it keeps an endnode table of (MAC, Data Label, egress switch nickname) entries for remote addresses its endnodes are talking to. Entries can be configured, received through ESADI, looked up in a directory, or learned by decapsulating traffic.

With many remote endnodes the table could become very large. And if a MAC address and Data Label have moved to another remote switch, the edge RBridge may be slow to notice, so it encapsulates to the wrong egress RBridge and the traffic is lost. This RFC addresses both the size and the freshness of the table.
sections.eli5: A switch that remembers every device it has talked to has a very long list, and the list can be wrong if someone moves. Letting devices keep their own lists shrinks the switch's list.

sections.title: The Smart Endnode Idea
sections.content:
An endnode E attached to an edge RBridge R tells R that it wants to be a Smart Endnode. E then encapsulates and decapsulates TRILL frames itself, using R's nickname, so no extra nicknames are consumed. Only the attached edge RBridge can tell a Smart Endnode from a normal one.

In the RFC's example, SE1 and SE2 attach to RB1, which assigns one of its nicknames for them to use. Each keeps a table of (MAC, Data Label, egress nickname) for remote endnodes it talks to. RB1 does not decapsulate packets for them and does not learn entries for their correspondents, though it still does so for attached endnodes that are not Smart.

Smart Endnodes learn and time out entries like RBridges do, but may also delete an entry early, for example when ICMP messages or other techniques show it is not reaching the destination. If there is no entry, the Smart Endnode encapsulates the packet as an unknown destination or consults a directory.

A Smart Endnode can use a Fine-Grained Label as the inner label, so the method supports FGL-aware endnodes. How it decides between FGL and VLAN is out of scope. A Smart Endnode does not send or receive LSPs and does not compute topology.
sections.eli5: A smart guest wears the front desk's name tag when sending packages, so the packages look like they came from the desk. It also keeps its own notes on where to send things.

sections.title: Smart-Hello Messages
sections.content:
Smart Endnodes and supporting edge RBridges talk through Smart-Hellos, a type of TRILL ES-IS PDU defined in RFC 8171. The payload is made of TRILL IS-IS TLVs, using the non-extended format with 8-bit type and size fields. Both kinds of Smart-Hello MUST include a Smart-Parameters APPsub-TLV (type 22, length 4) inside a TRILL GENINFO TLV. It carries a 2-byte Holding Time and 2 bytes of Flags that are all reserved: send zero, ignore on receipt.

The sender MUST send a Smart-Hello at least three times during its Holding Time. If none arrive within the most recent Holding Time, the sender is assumed to be gone. If a Smart-Hello has more than one Smart-Parameters, the first is used. If it has none, the Smart-Hello is ignored.

The edge RBridge's Smart-Hello also reuses, from RFC 7176, its nickname sub-TLV (inside TLV 242, first one used), the Tree Identifiers sub-TLV, and the TRILL Neighbor TLV as the Smart Endnode neighbor list. An Authentication TLV MAY be included.

The Smart Endnode's Smart-Hello adds a new Smart-MAC APPsub-TLV (type 23) listing MAC addresses for one VLAN or FGL. Its Length is 4+6*n for n addresses. The F bit says the label is an FGL, the M bit signals multihoming, and 6 bits are reserved. With F equal to 1 the 24-bit label is an FGL, otherwise the low 12 bits are the VLAN. Several VLANs or FGLs mean several Smart-MAC TLVs.
sections.eli5: Smart-Hello is a 'hello, here I am' note. The guest says which devices it speaks for, and the desk answers with its own name tag and the list of guests it knows.

sections.title: How a Smart Endnode Sends Data
sections.content:
All TRILL Data packets to or from Smart Endnodes are sent in the Designated VLAN of the local link, though they need not be VLAN tagged. The Smart Endnode fills its table the same way an edge RBridge does: by learning from the source MAC and ingress nickname of packets it decapsulates, by querying a directory, or from configuration.

  • For a known unicast destination, it uses RB1's nickname as ingress and the table entry's nickname as egress.
  • For an unknown destination, it queries a directory or encapsulates as a multi-destination frame using one of the trees RB1 named in its Smart-Hello.
  • For broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic, it uses one of those trees. The outer destination MAC is the All-RBridges multicast address.

A Smart Endnode need not send Smart-Hellos as often as RBridges, and may unicast them to the Appointed Forwarder. If RB1 restarts or the DRB changes and the Smart Endnode sees a Smart-Hello that does not mention it, it SHOULD send one immediately. If RB1 is Appointed Forwarder for any VLAN the Smart Endnode claims, RB1 MUST list it as a Smart Endnode neighbor.
sections.eli5: The smart guest looks up where to send a package in its own notes. If it does not know, it asks a directory or sends the package out the general way the desk told it about.

sections.title: What the Edge RBridge Does
sections.content:
The edge RBridge treats Smart Endnode traffic differently from native frames.

  • An encapsulated unicast packet from a Smart Endnode is forwarded to the egress nickname as usual. RB1 SHOULD filter on the inner source MAC and Data Label and drop frames that do not match what the Smart Endnode declared. Without this check, a rogue end station can more easily inject bogus TRILL Data packets.
  • A unicast packet for a MAC listed by a Smart Endnode is left encapsulated and sent to it. The hop count is still decreased by 1, because there is one hop between RB1 and the Smart Endnode.
  • A multi-destination packet from a Smart Endnode is forwarded along the tree named by the egress nickname, and dropped if that nickname is not a tree. Normal endnodes on the same switch get a decapsulated copy.

Ports with both Smart and normal endnodes (hybrid) force the RBridge to send two copies of multi-destination frames, one native and one encapsulated. That adds complexity and wastes bandwidth, so it is RECOMMENDED to attach Smart and non-Smart endnodes to different ports.
sections.eli5: The desk checks that each smart guest only uses return addresses it announced. It hands packages over still wrapped, and keeps plain-mail guests on a separate doorway.

sections.title: Multihoming
sections.content:
A Smart Endnode may attach to the TRILL domain through two edge RBridges, RB1 and RB2, which can both announce their nicknames. It can pick either nickname, or use both for active-active load balancing, using RB1's nickname when sending through RB1 and RB2's when sending through RB2.

That causes MAC flip-flopping in the endnode tables of remote RBridges and Smart Endnodes, because the same MAC keeps appearing behind different nicknames. The proposed fix is a multihoming bit set in the packet. When a remote device sees it, the entries (MAC, label, RB1 nickname) and (MAC, label, RB2 nickname) coexist. The RFC mentions distributing multiple attachments with ESADI as an alternative.
sections.eli5: If a guest uses two doors, the others might keep changing which door they write down. A special mark says 'I really use both doors', so they write down both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Smart-Hellos can be secured with Authentication TLVs based on RFC 5310. If they are not, a rogue end station is more easily mistaken for a valid Smart Endnode. Ports may also require end stations to authenticate with IEEE 802.1X and protect traffic with IEEE 802.1AE.

A misbehaving Smart Endnode can forge ingress and egress nicknames, and inner and outer MAC addresses, and can send data in any Data Label. Egress devices that believe a forged ingress nickname may send later traffic for that inner source MAC to the wrong edge RBridge when data-plane learning is in use. Therefore a port should not support Smart Endnodes unless the end stations are trusted or adequately authenticated.

Smart Endnodes also learn MAC addresses of edge RBridges and egress nicknames, so they can learn a substantial amount about the topology, which is a risk if they are compromised. The RFC suggests considering end-to-end encryption and authentication as added protection.
sections.eli5: A smart guest can write whatever return address it likes on packages, so the desk should only allow guests it trusts or has checked.
